title: An interactive transport profile
text: This is a demonstration, not a real dataset. It shows the kind of interactive, well-documented analysis this site can host: a question, an explicit method, an explorable result and enough source to reproduce it.

title: An interactive transport profile
text:
The question
How does the shape of a daily travel profile change by mode, and what happens when the morning peak becomes more pronounced?
The chart below is generated in the reader’s browser with Observable JS. It needs no server and works on a static GitHub Pages site.

title: An interactive transport profile
An interactive transport profile
text:
What to look for
The demonstration deliberately separates three elements:

The baseline represents movement that occurs throughout the day.
Two Gaussian peaks represent morning and evening demand.
The control applies the same multiplier to both peaks, making the assumption visible and easy to challenge.

Changing mode swaps in a different set of synthetic parameters. Walking has a flatter profile; bus travel has stronger commute peaks; cycling sits between them. These are illustrative shapes only, not empirical estimates.

About
text:
I’m James Hulse, a data scientist based in Manchester. I work with data to understand transport, infrastructure and place, using tools including R, Python and spatial analysis.
This site is my space for publishing work in the open. Some pieces will be short notes; others will be full reproducible vignettes with code, data provenance, assumptions and interactive outputs. The aim is simple: make the route from question to conclusion visible.

title: A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
text:
Reproducibility is not achieved by adding a repository link at the end of an article. It starts with the way the analysis is organised and explained.
This is the default pattern I plan to use for longer technical pieces on this site.

title: A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
text:
1. Begin with a precise question
State what the analysis is trying to learn before introducing tools or data. A reader should be able to tell what would count as an answer—and what falls outside the scope.

title: A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
text:
2. Describe the evidence
Record each input’s source, coverage, retrieval date and licence. If a dataset changes over time, keep a stable snapshot or an exact version identifier.



Field
What to record




Source
Publisher and canonical URL


Coverage
Geography, dates and population


Version
Release, retrieval date or checksum


Licence
Reuse terms and attribution


Known limits
Gaps, biases and measurement issues

title: A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
text:
4. Put interpretation beside output
A chart does not explain itself. Describe the dominant pattern, the comparison that matters and the uncertainty that should temper the conclusion. Interactive controls should reveal a meaningful choice—not decorate the page.

title: A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
text:
5. Make rerunning realistic
For R or Python work, pin dependencies with renv or a Python environment file. Quarto’s frozen computations can preserve article outputs between runs, while the environment files explain how to recreate them.






Note



This site uses freeze: auto. When a computational article is rendered locally, its results can be committed in _freeze/; the publishing action can then rebuild the website without rerunning every historical analysis.

title: A practical pattern for reproducible vignettes
text:
6. Finish with boundaries
Say what the analysis cannot establish, what would change the conclusion, and what should be tried next. That final section is often more useful than a polished summary.
The template in this repository turns these headings into a practical starting point for the next vignette.
